docs.title: corm
docs.text: corm wraps nested dictionaries from parsed JSON or YAML in lightweight Python entities. If you've ever needed to get the parent of a nested model, corm gives the child a back-reference to its parent. It also resolves ID references through an in-memory identity map. corm wraps the input dictionaries in place without copying or validating them. Undeclared keys are preserved, and dict() exports the data as dictionaries again.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A project API returns users and sprints. Each sprint embeds its tasks, and each task stores an assignee_id. The example follows both links, moves a task to a new sprint, and checks that the export preserves the task's assignee and undeclared keys such as labels.

Download the runnable project example.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str
    tasks: list["Task"] = Relationship()


class Task(Entity):
    title: str
    assignee: User = KeyNested(User.id, origin="assignee_id", back_populates="tasks")
    sprint: "Sprint | None" = Relationship()


class Sprint(Entity):
    name: str
    tasks: list[Task] = Nested(back_populates="sprint")


class Project(Entity):
    name: str
    users: list[User] = Nested()
    sprints: list[Sprint] = Nested()


payload = {
    "name": "Customer portal",
    "archived": False,
    "users": [{"id": 42, "name": "Amina", "timezone": "UTC"}],
    "sprints": [
        {
            "name": "Sprint 12",
            "tasks": [
                {
                    "title": "Add invoice download",
                    "assignee_id": 42,
                    "labels": ["billing"],
                }
            ],
        },
        {"name": "Sprint 13", "tasks": []},
    ],
}

project = Project(payload, Storage())
current_sprint, next_sprint = project.sprints
(task,) = current_sprint.tasks
(user,) = project.users

assert project.name == "Customer portal"
assert task.title == "Add invoice download"
assert task.sprint is current_sprint
assert task.assignee is user
assert user.tasks == [task]

task.sprint = next_sprint

assert current_sprint.tasks == []
assert next_sprint.tasks == [task]
assert task.sprint is next_sprint
assert task.assignee is user
assert user.tasks == [task]

assert project.dict() == {
    "name": "Customer portal",
    "archived": False,
    "users": [{"id": 42, "name": "Amina", "timezone": "UTC"}],
    "sprints": [
        {"name": "Sprint 12", "tasks": []},
        {
            "name": "Sprint 13",
            "tasks": [
                {
                    "title": "Add invoice download",
                    "assignee_id": 42,
                    "labels": ["billing"],
                }
            ],
        },
    ],
}

docs.title: When to use corm
docs.text:
Use corm to edit a document in memory when your code often navigates from a child to its parent or follows references by ID. corm is not a validation library and is not optimized for speed. Choose a validation or decoding library for untrusted input, a dot-access wrapper for simple attribute access, or SQLite with an ORM when you need queries, joins, or transactions.

Tool Validation Back-references References by ID Preserves unknown keys Typed attribute access corm No Built in with back_populates Built in with KeyNested Yes, by default Yes, for declared fields Pydantic Yes Application code Application code With extra="allow" Yes attrs + cattrs / msgspec attrs validators / typed decoding in msgspec Application code Application code Requires explicit handling Yes python-box No Application code Application code Yes, as mapping keys Dynamic dot access In-memory SQLite + ORM Database constraints With mapped relationships With foreign keys and joins Explicit storage, such as a JSON column With typed ORM models

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install with pip install corm. corm is in early development, and its API may change.

See the entity guide to define your own entities, or read the changelog for recent changes.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to corm are documented here. The format follows Keep a Changelog.

The library API and behavior from 0.0.7 carry forward into 0.1.0. The release audit verified the following public contracts:

  • Paired relationships via back_populates and continued support for deprecated back_relation declarations.
  • Document-scoped Storage.rekey() with conflict checks before writes.
  • Typed Storage.iter_entities() with subclass inclusion, identity deduplication and unspecified iteration order.
  • Persistent append() on unpaired KeyNested lists, preserving existing records and unresolved references.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Add Storage.iter_entities to enumerate indexed entities by type. (#5)

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Add document-scoped Storage.rekey to rewrite a primary key and its loaded document references. (#9)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • Persist appends to unpaired KeyNested lists while preserving existing raw records and unresolved references. (#75)

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Omit top-level output keys with entity.dict(exclude=["id"]). (#7)
  • Add runnable recipes for request-scoped storage, copying and renumbering a document, and transforming input and output with FastAPI or cattrs.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Allocate paired-list revision counters on the first edit. On CPython 3.14.5, retained Python allocations fell by 13.9% in the read benchmark and 2.2% in the benchmark that removes and restores each link. (#65)

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Pair a Nested or KeyNested field with a reverse Relationship using back_populates. Editing either side updates both fields. (#33)
  • Infer the related entity type and whether it is a list from annotations. (#32)
  • Ship a py.typed marker and expose a CormError hierarchy for library errors. (#34)
  • Automate PyPI publishing and GitHub Releases from version tags. (#29)
  • Add runnable documentation examples and benchmarks for document setup and traversal. (#35, #36)

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Require Python 3.11 or newer and test on Python 3.11 through 3.15. Use uv, Ruff, and pre-commit for development. (#28)
  • Expose AccessMode as a combinable IntFlag. (#34)
  • Update paired list relationships incrementally on append and remove. Repeated owner.targets.append(item) calls can reuse unretained list views on GIL-enabled CPython. Previously retained views and dictionary exports keep their contents. (#42)

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text: • Use back_populates for new reverse links. The back_relation argument remains available and emits a deprecation warning. (#33)

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • Remove the unused corm.hooks module. (#27)

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Preserve nested entity data when exporting dictionaries. Fix field inference and relationship reassignment, and reject duplicate keys before loading relationships for the duplicate entity. (#27)
  • Resolve relationships to instances of subclasses of the declared type. (#30)
  • Keep primary-key lookup in sync with key changes and keep relation reads from changing the index. Index relation membership while preserving order. (#31)
  • Preserve raw input keys that share a name with a Relationship field when exporting an entity with dict(). (#40)
  • Allow a redefined owner class to take over its back_populates pair. Instances of the previous class are stale after the handoff. (#41)

docs.title: Is corm fast or memory-efficient?
docs.text:
corm is designed for convenient navigation and editing of related data in memory. It is not optimized for speed. The storage keeps references to the entities it indexes and the entities in its relation index.

The benchmark measures setup and relationship traversal for dictionaries and corm entities.

docs.title: Does corm validate input?
docs.text: corm uses annotations for typed attribute access and relation inference. It checks that required fields are present and that it can maintain declared relationships and keys. It does not validate field value types or coerce data.

docs.title: How is this different from Pydantic?
docs.text: Pydantic validates and parses input into typed models. If you want a nested child to know its parent in Pydantic, you set up that link in application code. corm gives the child a parent link through a paired Nested and Relationship and resolves references by ID through Storage. It works directly with the input dictionary and preserves undeclared keys by default.

docs.title: Can I use it with Pydantic or attrs models?
docs.text:
Yes. Validate or structure your input first, then pass a dictionary from model_dump() or attrs.asdict() into corm. Use output keys that match your corm fields' origin settings. You can also pass entity.dict() back to your validation or structuring layer. corm wraps the dictionaries you pass in, so edits through corm update those dictionaries.

For a runnable HTTP endpoint, see Reassign a task with FastAPI.

docs.title: Open feature requests
docs.text:
Stages 0–2 of the roadmap shipped in Corm 0.0.4, including documentation and benchmarks.

The following proposals are candidates for stage 3. Work begins when an external user requests a feature for a concrete use case.

  • Query API
  • Exclude fields during entity creation

For entities with the same class name in different modules, see Models with the same name. For independent requests or jobs, see Storage for concurrent work. To create an independent graph, see Copy a document into another store.

docs.title: Accept two ID spellings and redact a nested field
docs.text:
A member import accepts either memberId or id. Other code looks up the member by its canonical id. A response includes the member's profile and omits its internal note. The note must remain available for later edits.

load_member copies the payload because corm wraps nested dictionaries in place. It rejects ambiguous IDs before constructing or registering the member. export_member removes the note from the dictionary that corm exported for the declared Nested profile. Other keys pass through. If the response has a fixed set of public fields, select those fields explicitly.

from collections.abc import Callable
from copy import deepcopy
from typing import Any

from corm import Entity, Field, Nested, Storage


class Profile(Entity):
    name: str
    internal_note: str


class Member(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    profile: Profile = Nested()


def load_member(payload: dict[str, Any], storage: Storage) -> Member:
    data = deepcopy(payload)
    if "memberId" in data:
        if "id" in data:
            raise ValueError("Supply either memberId or id")
        data["id"] = data.pop("memberId")
    return Member(data, storage)


def export_member(member: Member) -> dict[str, Any]:
    data = member.dict()
    del data["profile"]["internal_note"]
    return data


def check_transforms(
    load: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Member],
    export: Callable[[Member], dict[str, Any]],
) -> None:
    payload = {
        "memberId": 7,
        "profile": {"name": "Amina", "internal_note": "Confirm spelling"},
    }
    original = deepcopy(payload)
    member = load(payload)
    assert member.storage.get(Member.id, 7) is member
    assert export(member) == {"id": 7, "profile": {"name": "Amina"}}
    assert member.profile.internal_note == "Confirm spelling"
    assert member.dict() == {"id": 7, "profile": original["profile"]}
    assert payload == original

    canonical = {"id": 8, "profile": original["profile"]}
    assert load(canonical).id == 8
    try:
        load({**canonical, "memberId": 7})
    except ValueError as exc:
        assert str(exc) == "Supply either memberId or id"
    else:
        raise AssertionError("Ambiguous IDs must be rejected")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    check_transforms(lambda payload: load_member(payload, Storage()), export_member)

Run the example from the repository root with uv run --locked python -m docs.examples.document_transforms.

docs.title: Use the same policy with cattrs
docs.text:
An application that already uses a cattrs Converter can register the two functions for Member. Each structure call below loads one independent document into a fresh store. The unstructure hook applies the response policy when cattrs exports a member. Other code can still call member.dict() for a full export.

from cattrs import Converter

from corm import Storage
from docs.examples.document_transforms import (
    Member,
    check_transforms,
    export_member,
    load_member,
)

converter = Converter()
converter.register_structure_hook(Member, lambda data, _: load_member(data, Storage()))
converter.register_unstructure_hook(Member, export_member)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    check_transforms(
        lambda data: converter.structure(data, Member), converter.unstructure
    )

Run the same assertions through cattrs with uv run --locked --with cattrs==26.2.1 python -m docs.recipes.cattrs_transforms.

docs.title: Reassign a task with FastAPI
docs.text:
This endpoint accepts a task, its current and prospective owners, and the ID of the new owner. It returns the edited task with the names of both owners. Each request supplies its own data, so the endpoint also works as a preview without a database.

From the repository root, start the example:

uv run --locked --group fastapi-example uvicorn --port 8765 --app-dir docs/recipes fastapi_app:app

Send a request in another terminal:

curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8765/tasks/reassign \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"users":[{"id":1,"name":"Amina"},{"id":2,"name":"Lee"}],"task":{"title":"Invoice","ownerId":1,"internal":"private note"},"new_owner_id":2}'

{"title":"Invoice","ownerId":2,"previous_owner":"Amina","owner_name":"Lee"}

docs.title: From HTTP fields to linked entities
docs.text:
Pydantic reads the JSON key ownerId into TaskInput.owner_id. model_dump(by_alias=True) restores the wire name in the dictionary that Corm wraps. The KeyNested field resolves that key to a User in the request's Storage. Assigning a different user to task.owner writes the new ID back to the dictionary. A subsequent request can reuse the same numeric IDs for other users because it creates a fresh store.

Task input accepts extra keys such as internal. Corm preserves them during the edit. FastAPI filters the exported dictionary through TaskReply, which declares the public response fields. Invalid IDs, missing owners and duplicate user IDs produce HTTP 422.

from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
from pydantic import Field as WireField

from corm import (
    DuplicateKeyError,
    Entity,
    EntityNotFoundError,
    Field,
    KeyNested,
    Storage,
)


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str


class Task(Entity):
    title: str
    owner: User = KeyNested(User.id, origin="ownerId")


class UserInput(BaseModel):
    id: int
    name: str


class TaskInput(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")
    title: str
    owner_id: int = WireField(alias="ownerId")


class Reassignment(BaseModel):
    users: list[UserInput]
    task: TaskInput
    new_owner_id: int


class TaskReply(BaseModel):
    title: str
    owner_id: int = WireField(alias="ownerId")
    previous_owner: str
    owner_name: str


app = FastAPI()


@app.post("/tasks/reassign", response_model=TaskReply)
def reassign(body: Reassignment):
    storage = Storage()
    try:
        for member in body.users:
            User(member.model_dump(), storage)
        task = Task(body.task.model_dump(by_alias=True), storage)
        previous_owner = task.owner.name
    except (DuplicateKeyError, EntityNotFoundError) as exc:
        raise HTTPException(
            422, "User IDs must be unique and include the task owner"
        ) from exc

    new_owner = storage.get(User.id, body.new_owner_id)
    if not isinstance(new_owner, User):
        raise HTTPException(422, "Unknown new owner")
    task.owner = new_owner
    return {
        **task.dict(),
        "previous_owner": previous_owner,
        "owner_name": task.owner.name,
    }

The fastapi-example dependency group provides the HTTP tools for this recipe. Installing corm alone keeps the library's runtime dependencies empty. To exercise the endpoint in process:

uv run --locked --group fastapi-example --group test pytest -q docs/recipes/test_fastapi_app.py

docs.title: Entities
docs.text: An Entity wraps a dictionary. Declare the fields you want to access as attributes, then pass the dictionary and a Storage to the entity constructor. Attribute writes update the wrapped dictionary. Undeclared keys stay in the data and are included in entity.dict().

docs.title: Field declarations
docs.text: An explicit Field or relation descriptor becomes a field. A public annotation such as name: str declares a field, and a public class value such as description = "Project member" supplies a default. Unannotated methods, properties, other callables, and names starting with _ stay out of the implicit field declarations. Annotations describe field types for editors and type checkers. corm uses relation annotations to infer related entity types and whether a field holds one entity or a list.

docs.title: Input and output keys
docs.text: origin is the dictionary key a field reads and writes. It defaults to the attribute name. destination is the key used by dict() and defaults to origin. When they differ, the export uses the destination key in place of the origin. Load the export with a model that expects the destination key, or map it back before reloading with the same model.

docs.title: Filtering input before construction
docs.text:
To drop import-only data, filter the source keys before calling the entity constructor. Copy retained nested values if the caller needs to reuse the original payload. corm wraps those dictionaries in place.

Source key removed in this example Result Undeclared import_batch The member and its badge load. The extra key is absent from the export. Optional badges The field takes its empty-list default. The export includes badges: [], and the store contains no badge. Required primary key id Construction raises MissingFieldError before loading the badge. Required display_name (exported as name) Construction raises MissingFieldError. The badge loaded earlier is already registered in the supplied store.

For an independent document that must load as a unit, construct it in a fresh store and keep that store only after the constructor succeeds. To keep an ID available for lookups and omit it only from a response, see Access and export.

from copy import deepcopy
from typing import Any

from corm import Entity, Field, MissingFieldError, Nested, Storage


class Badge(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)


class Member(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    badges: list[Badge] = Nested(default=list)
    name: str = Field(origin="display_name", destination="name")


def load_member(payload: dict[str, Any], storage: Storage, *omit: str) -> Member:
    data = {key: deepcopy(value) for key, value in payload.items() if key not in omit}
    return Member(data, storage)


payload = {
    "id": 7,
    "display_name": "Amina",
    "badges": [{"id": 42}],
    "import_batch": "November",
}
original = deepcopy(payload)

store = Storage()
member = load_member(payload, store, "import_batch")
assert member.dict() == {"id": 7, "name": "Amina", "badges": [{"id": 42}]}
assert store.get(Member.id, 7) is member
assert store.get(Badge.id, 42) is member.badges[0]

store = Storage()
member = load_member(payload, store, "import_batch", "badges")
assert member.dict() == {"id": 7, "name": "Amina", "badges": []}
assert store.get(Member.id, 7) is member
assert store.get(Badge.id, 42) is None

for required_key in ("id", "display_name"):
    candidate = Storage()
    try:
        load_member(payload, candidate, required_key)
    except MissingFieldError:
        assert candidate.get(Member.id, 7) is None
    else:
        raise AssertionError(f"Expected a missing field for {required_key}")

    # The primary key loads first. In this model badges load before the name.
    badge = candidate.get(Badge.id, 42)
    if required_key == "id":
        assert badge is None
    else:
        assert isinstance(badge, Badge) and badge.id == 42

assert payload == original

docs.title: Access and export
docs.text:
Field and Nested default to AccessMode.ALL. Combine AccessMode flags with |. LOAD processes the field at construction, SET permits assignment, and DUMP exports the field through its declared destination. The GET flag describes a readable field. The current descriptors still allow direct reads without it. KeyNested defaults to GET_SET_LOAD so the original key stays in the exported data. A reverse Relationship lives in the relation index.

dict(strip_none=True) omits declared fields with DUMP whose value is None, including fields in declared nested entities. Undeclared keys with None values are preserved.

Pass exclude=["id", "timezone"] to omit top-level keys from the exported dictionary. Use the emitted key (the destination for a field with DUMP). A single string names one key. Missing keys are ignored, and nested dictionaries keep their own keys. Calling dict() again returns the full export. This option was added in 0.0.5.

The example reads an ID from user_id, exports it as id, and uses a read-only display name. It also shows an optional field and an undeclared key.

from corm import AccessMode, Entity, Field, ReadOnlyFieldError, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(origin="user_id", destination="id")
    name: str = Field(mode=AccessMode.GET | AccessMode.LOAD | AccessMode.DUMP)
    description: str = "Project member"
    nickname: str | None = Field(default=None)


payload = {"user_id": 33, "name": "Amina", "timezone": "UTC", "metadata": None}
user = User(payload, Storage())

assert user.id == 33
user.id = 34
assert payload["user_id"] == 34
assert user.name == "Amina"

try:
    user.name = "Mina"
except ReadOnlyFieldError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("The name field is read-only")

assert user.dict() == {
    "id": 34,
    "name": "Amina",
    "description": "Project member",
    "nickname": None,
    "timezone": "UTC",
    "metadata": None,
}
assert user.dict(strip_none=True) == {
    "id": 34,
    "name": "Amina",
    "description": "Project member",
    "timezone": "UTC",
    "metadata": None,
}
assert user.dict(strip_none=True, exclude=["id", "timezone"]) == {
    "name": "Amina",
    "description": "Project member",
    "metadata": None,
}

docs.title: Default values
docs.text:
Supply a plain class value or pass default= to Field, Nested, or KeyNested. corm calls a default factory for each instance whose input lacks that field. An explicit None value in the input counts as a supplied value.

from corm import Entity, Field, Storage


class Foo(Entity):
    inplace = 1
    in_field = Field(default=2)
    in_field_callable = Field(default=list)


storage = Storage()
foo = Foo(data={}, storage=storage)

assert foo.inplace == 1
assert foo.in_field == 2
assert foo.in_field_callable == []

A callable assigned directly to the class remains a class attribute. Use Field(default=list) if you want corm to call list as a field's default factory.

from corm import Entity, Storage


class Foo(Entity):
    inplace = list


storage = Storage()
foo = Foo(data={}, storage=storage)

assert foo.inplace is list  # still callable, not new empty list

docs.title: Key relationships
docs.text: KeyNested takes the related entity's primary-key field as its related_entity_field argument. It infers many=True from list annotations such as list[Address] or list["Address"]. You can still pass many= to set this explicitly.

docs.title: Resolve a list of keys
docs.text:
Use origin when the input key name differs from the attribute name. This example reads the entity_ids list and resolves each ID to a stored entity. Access the resulting list through holder.entities.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Storage


class SomeEntity(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str


class EntityHolder(Entity):
    name: str
    entities: list[SomeEntity] = KeyNested(
        related_entity_field=SomeEntity.id,
        origin="entity_ids",
    )


storage = Storage()
entity = SomeEntity({"id": 123, "name": "entity"}, storage=storage)
holder = EntityHolder({"entity_ids": [123], "name": "holder"}, storage=storage)

assert holder.entities == [entity]

docs.title: Bidirectional key relationships
docs.text:
Set back_populates on KeyNested to name the Relationship on the entity referenced by the key. The reverse field's annotation or many= setting controls whether it returns a single owner or a list of owners. An owner can be loaded before the related entity. Its reverse link is available when that key appears in storage.

If the target inherits its primary-key field, annotate the KeyNested attribute with the target subclass to select its Relationship.

from corm import (
    Entity,
    Field,
    KeyNested,
    Relationship,
    Storage,
)


class SomeEntity(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str
    holder: "EntityHolder | None" = Relationship()


class EntityHolder(Entity):
    name: str
    entity: SomeEntity = KeyNested(
        related_entity_field=SomeEntity.id,
        origin="entity_id",
        back_populates="holder",
    )


storage = Storage()
holder = EntityHolder({"name": "holder", "entity_id": 123}, storage=storage)
entity = SomeEntity({"id": 123, "name": "entity"}, storage=storage)

assert holder.entity == entity
assert entity.holder == holder

docs.title: Change relationships between entities
docs.text:
Writing through either field updates the owner's stored key. Assign an owner to a single Relationship to move the link, or assign None to clear it. For a reverse list, append or remove owners or assign the replacement list. If the owning KeyNested field is a list, the operation adds or removes the corresponding key. With required=False, edits to the list of resolved entities preserve keys that are still missing. Assigning a replacement list directly to the owning field replaces its stored keys.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Relationship, Storage


class SomeEntity(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str
    holder: "EntityHolder | None" = Relationship()


class EntityHolder(Entity):
    entity: SomeEntity | None = KeyNested(
        related_entity_field=SomeEntity.id,
        origin="entity_id",
        back_populates="holder",
    )


storage = Storage()
entity1 = SomeEntity({"id": 123, "name": "entity1"}, storage=storage)
entity2 = SomeEntity({"id": 321, "name": "entity2"}, storage=storage)
holder = EntityHolder(
    data={"entity_id": 123},
    storage=storage,
)

holder.entity = entity2

assert entity1.holder is None
assert entity2.holder is holder
assert holder.entity is entity2
assert holder.dict() == {"entity_id": 321}

new_holder = EntityHolder({"entity_id": None}, storage)
entity2.holder = new_holder

assert holder.entity is None
assert holder.dict() == {"entity_id": None}
assert new_holder.entity is entity2
assert new_holder.dict() == {"entity_id": 321}

docs.title: Keys stored as objects
docs.text:
Pass a KeyManager when a reference is stored in a shape other than a bare key. Implement get(data) to extract the hashable key used by Storage and prepare_to_set(entity) to produce the stored representation when assigning an entity. A list relation calls these methods for each reference. Return None from prepare_to_set(None) for a cleared single reference.

This example reads and writes team member references stored as objects such as {"entity_id": 123}. The reference key can differ from the primary-key field on the related entity. Loading and exporting keeps extra keys such as rank on the original reference. Replacing the whole list calls prepare_to_set for each assigned entity, so the new references contain only what that method returns.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyManager, KeyNested, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)


class UserKeyManager(KeyManager):
    def get(self, data: dict[str, int]) -> int:
        return data["entity_id"]

    def prepare_to_set(self, entity: Entity | None) -> dict[str, int] | None:
        if entity is None:
            return None
        assert isinstance(entity, User)
        return {"entity_id": entity.id}


class Team(Entity):
    members: list[User] = KeyNested(
        User.id, origin="member_refs", key_manager=UserKeyManager()
    )


storage = Storage()
amina = User({"id": 123}, storage)
lee = User({"id": 456}, storage)
team = Team({"member_refs": [{"entity_id": 123, "rank": 1}]}, storage)

assert team.members == [amina]
assert team.dict() == {"member_refs": [{"entity_id": 123, "rank": 1}]}

team.members = [amina, lee]

assert team.members == [amina, lee]
assert team.dict() == {"member_refs": [{"entity_id": 123}, {"entity_id": 456}]}

docs.title: Keeping metadata when a list changes
docs.text:
Suppose two references to user 1 have ranks 10 and 11. Assigning a list containing just that user gives a key manager the same User object for either choice. If the caller needs to keep the rank-11 entry, model each reference as a nested entity with its own rank and a KeyNested link to the user. The caller can then select the exact membership to keep. An unresolved membership can also be kept explicitly until its user loads.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Nested, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)


class Membership(Entity):
    user: User | None = KeyNested(User.id, origin="entity_id", required=False)
    rank: int


class Team(Entity):
    members: list[Membership] = Nested()


storage = Storage()
amina = User({"id": 1}, storage)
lee = User({"id": 2}, storage)
team = Team(
    {
        "members": [
            {"entity_id": 1, "rank": 10},
            {"entity_id": 9, "rank": 90},
            {"entity_id": 1, "rank": 11},
        ]
    },
    storage,
)
first, pending, second = team.members
assert first.user is second.user is amina
assert pending.user is None

new_member = Membership({"entity_id": 2, "rank": 20}, storage)
team.members = [second, new_member, pending]
assert team.dict() == {
    "members": [
        {"entity_id": 1, "rank": 11},
        {"entity_id": 2, "rank": 20},
        {"entity_id": 9, "rank": 90},
    ]
}
assert new_member.user is lee
late_user = User({"id": 9}, storage)
assert pending.user is late_user

For an existing list[User] field backed by object-shaped keys, choose the operation according to the intended edit:

Operation Effect on the stored references Assign a plain list, e.g. team.users = [lee, amina] Rebuilds the key objects through prepare_to_set. Drops old references absent from the replacement, including unresolved IDs. Edit a paired field, e.g. team.users[:] = [lee, amina] With back_populates and required=False, keeps the old key objects for retained users and keeps unresolved references. New users get new key objects. Duplicate targets raise RelationError. Edit the result of an unpaired lookup, e.g. team.users.reverse() Reorders a temporary list. The stored references keep their original order and metadata.

docs.title: Rewriting a stored key
docs.text:
A custom KeyManager can opt in to key rewriting by implementing rewrite_key(record, new_key). The caller passes a detached copy of the stored record. The method returns a record whose get() value is new_key, preserves the other fields, and confines any in-place edits to the copy. The standard key manager returns the new key directly. Custom managers that leave the method unimplemented continue to support normal reads and writes.

This method prepares one record. Storage.rekey uses it before applying any changes to the graph.

docs.title: Nested relationships
docs.text:
Nested() and Relationship() infer the related entity type and whether the field holds one entity or a list. Use Address for a single entity and list[Address] for a list. Quoted forward references such as "Address" and list["Address"] are resolved through the entity registry when needed. Optional annotations such as Address | None and Optional[list[Address]] infer the same type and cardinality as their non-optional forms.

You can still pass entity_type= and many= explicitly. Each explicit argument overrides the corresponding inference.

docs.title: Simple relationship
docs.text:
Nested wraps an embedded dictionary as an entity, so a user can access the address fields through user.address.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Storage


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    number: int


class User(Entity):
    name: str
    address: Address = Nested()


storage = Storage()
john = User(
    data={
        "name": "John",
        "address": {
            "street": "First",
            "number": 1,
        },
    },
    storage=storage,
)

assert john.address.street == "First"
assert john.address.number == 1

docs.title: Models with the same name
docs.text:
Suppose billing and support each define an Account class. Import both modules so their class definitions register with Corm, then give each Nested field its target's full name (__module__ plus __qualname__). A string such as "Account" alone raises RegistryError when the field first resolves it and both classes are registered. The error lists the matching full names.

from account_models import billing, support

from corm import Entity, Nested, RegistryError, Storage


class Customer(Entity):
    payer: billing.Account = Nested("account_models.billing.Account")
    contact: support.Account = Nested("account_models.support.Account")


customer = Customer(
    {"payer": {"invoice_email": "a@example.org"}, "contact": {"queue": "returns"}},
    Storage(),
)
assert type(customer.payer) is billing.Account
assert type(customer.contact) is support.Account
assert customer.dict() == {
    "payer": {"invoice_email": "a@example.org"},
    "contact": {"queue": "returns"},
}

docs.title: Reloading a model module
docs.text:
Reloading account_models.billing registers a new class under the same full name. The existing payer keeps its original class. An unpaired Nested field that already resolved its target caches that class, so even a new Customer loaded in a fresh Storage still uses the original billing class. A newly declared owner with a fresh Nested field resolves the replacement. The support class keeps its identity throughout.

Run uv run python docs/examples/qualified_relationships.py from the repository root to exercise the two modules, the ambiguous short name and the reload.

docs.title: Bidirectional relationships
docs.text:
Set back_populates on the Nested field to name the Relationship on the related entity. Each pair has its own links, so fields such as Order.billing and Order.shipping can both point to Address and have separate reverse fields.

The reverse field's annotation or many= setting controls whether it returns one owner or a list of owners. corm resolves the pair when the first owning entity is created, which allows forward references. Target subclasses can use the pair by inheriting its Relationship.

When a redefined owner class takes over a back_populates pair, instances of the superseded class are stale and their behavior is undefined.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    number: int
    user: "User | None" = Relationship()


class User(Entity):
    name: str
    address: Address | None = Nested(back_populates="user")


storage = Storage()
john = User(
    data={
        "name": "John",
        "address": {
            "street": "First",
            "number": 1,
        },
    },
    storage=storage,
)

assert john.address is not None
assert john.address.user == john

docs.title: Self-nested
docs.text:
A pair can connect two fields on the same entity class. Appending a child to another parent's list or assigning its parent moves it from its old parent.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class Item(Entity):
    id: int
    items: list["Item"] = Nested(back_populates="parent", default=list)
    parent: "Item | None" = Relationship()


storage = Storage()
item1 = Item({"id": 1, "items": [{"id": 2}, {"id": 3}]}, storage)
item2, item3 = item1.items

assert item1.id == 1
assert item1.parent is None

assert item2.id == 2
assert item2.parent == item1
assert item2.items == []

assert item3.id == 3
assert item3.parent == item1
assert item3.items == []

item3.items.append(item2)
assert item2.parent is item3
assert item1.items == [item3]

item2.parent = item1
assert item1.items == [item3, item2]
assert item3.items == []

docs.title: Change relationships between entities
docs.text:
You can write through either field. Assign a new owner to a single Relationship to move the related entity, or assign None to unlink it. If the new owner holds a single value, the move replaces that value and clears the displaced entity's reverse link.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    user: "User | None" = Relationship()


class User(Entity):
    id: int
    address: Address | None = Nested(back_populates="user")


storage = Storage()
john = User(
    data={
        "id": 1,
        "name": "John",
        "description": "john smith",
        "address": {
            "street": "kirova",
        },
    },
    storage=storage,
)

old_address = john.address

assert old_address is not None
assert old_address.user is john

address = Address(data={"street": "lenina"}, storage=storage)
john.address = address

assert old_address.user is None
assert address.user is john
assert john.address is address

jane = User({"id": 2, "address": {"street": "First"}}, storage)
displaced = jane.address
assert displaced is not None
address.user = jane

assert john.address is None
assert jane.address is address
assert address.user is jane
assert displaced.user is None

address.user = None
assert jane.address is None
assert address.user is None

On either side, a list can be edited in place or replaced. Appending or removing an owner through a reverse list updates that owner's field.

from corm import Entity, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    users: list["User"] = Relationship()


class User(Entity):
    id: int
    addresses: list[Address] = Nested(back_populates="users", default=list)


storage = Storage()
john = User(
    data={
        "id": 1,
        "name": "John",
        "description": "john smith",
        "addresses": [
            {
                "street": "kirova 1",
            },
            {
                "street": "kirova 2",
            },
        ],
    },
    storage=storage,
)

old_address1, old_address2 = john.addresses

# you can change existing list
john.addresses.remove(old_address1)

assert old_address1.users == []
assert old_address2.users == [john]

john.addresses.clear()

assert old_address1.users == []
assert old_address2.users == []
assert john.addresses == []

new_address1 = Address(data={"street": "lenina 1"}, storage=storage)
new_address2 = Address(data={"street": "lenina 2"}, storage=storage)

john.addresses.append(new_address1)

assert new_address1.users == [john]
assert john.addresses == [new_address1]

john.addresses.extend([new_address2])

assert new_address2.users == [john]
assert john.addresses == [new_address1, new_address2]

# or completely replace it
john.addresses = [old_address1]

assert new_address1.users == []
assert new_address2.users == []
assert old_address1.users == [john]

jane = User({"id": 2}, storage)
old_address1.users.append(jane)
assert jane.addresses == [old_address1]

old_address1.users.remove(john)
assert john.addresses == []

old_address1.users = [john]
assert jane.addresses == []
assert john.addresses == [old_address1]

For an unpaired KeyNested(..., many=True), append(target) persists the key manager’s stored representation and preserves existing records, including unresolved keys. Other list edits (including extend, removal, and item assignment) affect only the returned list; assign the field to replace its stored value. A previously fetched list remains a snapshot, but its append still adds to the current stored records. Legacy back_relation appends also create reverse links and reject duplicate links.

The older back_relation parameter still works and emits a DeprecationWarning. To migrate, replace it with back_populates="reverse_field_name".

docs.title: Manually related entities
docs.text:
A standalone Relationship uses relation_type to read and write links managed directly by Storage. This example links a user to an address and then removes the link.

from corm import Entity, Relationship, RelationType, Storage

storage = Storage()


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    number: int


class User(Entity):
    name: str
    address: Address | None = Relationship(relation_type=RelationType.PARENT)


address = Address({"street": "First", "number": 1}, storage)
john = User({"name": "John"}, storage)

storage.make_relation(
    from_=john,
    to_=address,
    relation_type=RelationType.PARENT,
)

assert john.address == address

storage.remove_relation(
    from_=john,
    to_=address,
    relation_type=RelationType.PARENT,
)

assert john.address is None

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Storage is an in-memory identity map and relation index. Create one Storage() per loaded document and share it among that document's entities. Nested entities inherit their owner's storage. The storage holds strong references to indexed entities and relation endpoints, so they can live as long as the storage does, even after you drop your own references to them.

docs.title: Storage for concurrent work
docs.text:
Create the store where your application starts processing a document. Pass it to the functions that construct or look up its entities. An HTTP handler, a queue consumer and a batch job can all use the same functions. If a request contains two documents with independent ID spaces, give each its own store.

In this example two tasks load different users with ID 7. The barrier makes both tasks finish registering their user before either resolves its ticket. Each ticket finds the user from its own document.

import asyncio

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    name: str


class Ticket(Entity):
    owner: User = KeyNested(User.id, origin="owner_id")


async def process(name: str, storage: Storage, ready: asyncio.Barrier) -> str:
    user = User({"id": 7, "name": name}, storage)
    await ready.wait()  # Both documents have registered user 7.
    ticket = Ticket({"owner_id": 7}, storage)
    assert ticket.owner is user
    return ticket.owner.name


async def main() -> None:
    ready = asyncio.Barrier(2)
    names = await asyncio.gather(
        process("Amina", Storage(), ready),
        process("Lee", Storage(), ready),
    )
    assert names == ["Amina", "Lee"]


asyncio.run(main())

When a child task continues work on the same document, pass it the same store deliberately. For an independent job, create a fresh store in that job. If an application uses a Python ContextVar to carry the store, asyncio.create_task() copies the binding by default. The child still holds the same mutable Storage after the parent resets its binding. Resetting the parent's context cannot undo writes the child makes to that store.

The FastAPI recipe shows the same ownership rule in a web request.

docs.title: Copy a document into another store
docs.text:
To edit an independent copy, export the document root, deep-copy the payload, and load it into a fresh Storage. Include the owners and targets of the links you want to rebuild. In this example each board contains its own user 7 and ticket. Editing the copied ticket's labels leaves the original list intact. The deep copy matters because ordinary mutable field values can be shared with the dictionary returned by dict().

from copy import deepcopy

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Nested, Relationship, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    tickets: list["Ticket"] = Relationship()


class Ticket(Entity):
    owner: User = KeyNested(User.id, origin="owner_id", back_populates="tickets")
    labels: list[str]


class Board(Entity):
    users: list[User] = Nested()
    tickets: list[Ticket] = Nested()


source = Storage()
board = Board(
    {"users": [{"id": 7}], "tickets": [{"owner_id": 7, "labels": ["billing"]}]},
    source,
)
destination = Storage()
copied = Board(deepcopy(board.dict()), destination)

user, ticket = board.users[0], board.tickets[0]
new_user, new_ticket = copied.users[0], copied.tickets[0]
assert copied.dict() == board.dict()
assert source.get(User.id, 7) is user
assert destination.get(User.id, 7) is new_user
assert new_user is not user and new_ticket is not ticket
assert ticket.owner is user and user.tickets == [ticket]
assert new_ticket.owner is new_user and new_user.tickets == [new_ticket]

new_ticket.labels.append("reviewed")
assert ticket.labels == ["billing"]
assert new_ticket.labels == ["billing", "reviewed"]

Use this recipe for dictionary data that the destination model can load. If a field exports under a different key from the one it accepts, map the keys before loading. A KeyNested reference exports its stored ID with the default access mode. Copying a ticket alone makes it look up that ID in the destination. Supply the intended user there before reading the required link. Reverse links from paired fields are rebuilt when their owning data is loaded. Recreate manually indexed links separately.

A duplicate primary key raises DuplicateKeyError. In a multi-entity load, a child processed before the collision may already be indexed. If a failed import must leave a live graph intact, build the complete candidate in a fresh store, check the required links, and switch the application's root reference only after success. This replaces the graph with new Python objects. Existing references still point to the old ones.

Assigning entity.storage changes the attribute while the original store still indexes the object. Calling destination.add(entity) can then leave the same object indexed in both stores. Use reconstruction when you need independent graphs.

docs.title: Primary keys
docs.text:
Mark a field with Field(pk=True) to register each entity by that field and its value. storage.get(User.id, 1) returns the registered instance, or None if the key is absent. A key must be hashable. corm indexes each primary-key field separately, so two different fields can use the same key.

Creating another entity with the same key on the same field raises DuplicateKeyError. Assigning a new key through an entity attribute moves the index entry. A conflicting assignment raises the same error and leaves the original key and index entry in place.

docs.title: Enumerating indexed entities
docs.text:
store.iter_entities(User) lazily yields instances of User and its subclasses registered in this store's primary-key index. Each object appears once by identity, even if it has multiple primary-key entries. Entities without an index entry and pending references are excluded.

The iterator scans the live index. Index-changing writes, including adding entities or changing primary keys, must not overlap iteration. Result order is unspecified, including after rekeying. For repeatable ordering, use a stable, unique key, for example sorted(store.iter_entities(User), key=lambda u: u.id) when id meets those requirements. Collect the iterator into a list when a snapshot is needed.

docs.title: Finding the first matching entity
docs.text:
Choose the collection to search. A Python generator can filter a document's nested users, including users without primary keys. next(..., None) returns the first match in collection order or None if the name is absent. Creating another user in the same store leaves the document's list unchanged.

from collections.abc import Iterable

from corm import Entity, Field, Nested, Storage


class User(Entity):
    name: str


class Directory(Entity):
    users: list[User] = Nested()


def first_named(users: Iterable[User], name: str) -> User | None:
    return next((user for user in users if user.name == name), None)


store = Storage()
directory = Directory({"users": [{"name": "Lee"}, {"name": "Lee"}]}, store)
other = User({"name": "Amina"}, store)

assert first_named(directory.users, "Lee") is directory.users[0]
assert first_named(directory.users, "Amina") is None
assert first_named([other, *directory.users], "Amina") is other


class Member(User):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)


member = Member({"id": 7, "name": "Amina"}, store)
assert store.get(Member.id, 7) is member
assert store.get(Member.id, 8) is None

When the caller knows a primary key, store.get(Member.id, 7) goes directly to the identity index. An entity with two primary-key fields can be looked up through either field. A standalone user without a primary key has no entry in that index. For a name search, compare user.name on each instance. Comparing User.name to a string evaluates immediately to a boolean.

docs.title: Dangling key references
docs.text:
A KeyNested field can be loaded before its target. Each read looks up the stored key in the same storage. If the key is missing, reading the field raises EntityNotFoundError with the default required=True. Set required=False to return None for an unresolved single reference or skip unresolved keys in a list. The stored keys remain in the data.

Assigning a primary key through the entity attribute leaves existing references at their stored values. The example shows the old reference becoming unresolved and a reference waiting for the new key resolving to the same user.

from corm import Entity, Field, KeyNested, Relationship, Storage


class User(Entity):
    id: int = Field(pk=True)
    addresses: list["Address"] = Relationship()


class Address(Entity):
    user: User | None = KeyNested(
        User.id, origin="user_id", back_populates="addresses", required=False
    )


storage = Storage()
old_address = Address({"user_id": 1}, storage)
new_address = Address({"user_id": 5}, storage)
user = User({"id": 1}, storage)
assert old_address.user is user
assert new_address.user is None
owners_to_update = list(user.addresses)

user.id = 5

assert storage.get(User.id, 1) is None
assert storage.get(User.id, 5) is user
assert old_address.user is None
assert old_address.dict() == {"user_id": 1}
assert new_address.user is user
assert user.addresses == [new_address]

for address in owners_to_update:
    address.user = user

assert old_address.user is user
assert old_address.dict() == {"user_id": 5}
assert user.addresses == [new_address, old_address]

docs.title: Change a primary key and its references
docs.text:
To change a key and rewrite references in one loaded document, call store.rekey(root, target, User.id, new_id). The root and target must use this storage, and the target must be reachable from the root through loaded Nested fields (or be the root). The field must be the target's actual primary key descriptor, and its old key must resolve to that target. An occupied new key raises DuplicateKeyError.

The operation discovers scalar and list KeyNested records for that exact key field throughout the document and rewrites each occurrence of the old key. It preserves unpaired duplicates, list order, and custom record metadata. Pending references to other keys keep their stored values. An existing paired reference to the new key must accept the target entity type. Paired owners outside the root cause a RelationError if they would need rewriting; unpaired external references are outside the operation's scope and remain unchanged. Matching legacy back_relation fields and conflicting source aliases are rejected before any write. The primary key and references being rewritten must be writable. Paired duplicate and exclusive reverse conflicts are also rejected, including conflicts with pending references.

Exclusive access and a stable, valid graph are required throughout the call. Key managers must implement rewrite_key(record, new_key) and get for the rewritten record. They receive detached copies and must confine their writes to those inputs. All callbacks and conflict checks finish before data or indexes change; callback side effects outside their inputs and concurrent changes are outside this guarantee. Assigning a primary key normally retains the behavior described in Dangling key references.

docs.title: Renumbering a referenced entity
docs.text:
When the application knows the owners, it can keep the same Python object: capture the owners before changing its ID, change the ID, then reassign their key fields to the entity. The example above does this for scalar paired references. Include unpaired owners explicitly because they may have no reverse field. For a list of fully resolved plain keys, capture the ordered targets before the change and assign the list back afterwards. Whole-list assignment rebuilds the serialized keys. Omitted unresolved entries and extra metadata on rebuilt key objects can be lost.

When a document needs all edits to succeed together, prepare a replacement using its known schema. In this directory, user IDs appear in three places: the user records, the scalar lead_id, and the user_id in each group's ordered membership records. Change those keys in a deep copy so ranks, unrelated values and pending IDs survive. Load the candidate in a fresh store and check required links before replacing the application's root.

def renumber_user(directory: Directory, old_id: int, new_id: int) -> Directory:
    data = deepcopy(directory.dict())
    users = {user["id"]: user for user in data["users"]}
    users[old_id]["id"] = new_id
    if data["lead_id"] == old_id:
        data["lead_id"] = new_id
    for group in data["groups"]:
        for member in group["members"]:
            if member["user_id"] == old_id:
                member["user_id"] = new_id

    candidate = Directory(data, Storage())
    # Loading allows forward references. Resolve the required lead before handoff.
    if candidate.lead is None:
        raise ValueError("The directory needs a lead")
    return candidate

The runnable example changes user 1 to 5. Two other attempts fail: ID 2 belongs to another user, and ID 9 already appears as a pending member in the same paired list. The latter would create a duplicate membership. Both failures leave the original directory's data, lookups and reverse links intact. A reference already waiting for the new ID elsewhere can become resolved, as in the address example above. This application-level migration covers the directory passed to it and returns new Python objects.

docs.title: Manual relations
docs.text:
Use make_relation(from_=source, to_=target, relation_type=kind) to add a directed link for a standalone Relationship with a matching relation_type. Use remove_relation with the same arguments to unlink it. Adding an existing link or removing a missing one raises RelationError. For paired Nested and KeyNested fields, assign or edit the relation attributes to update the payload and index together.

get_related_entities() returns a new list in relation order. Editing that list leaves the storage index unchanged.

This example adds and removes a manual link from a user to an address.

from corm import Entity, Relationship, RelationType, Storage

storage = Storage()


class Address(Entity):
    street: str
    number: int


class User(Entity):
    name: str
    address: Address | None = Relationship(relation_type=RelationType.PARENT)


address = Address({"street": "First", "number": 1}, storage)
john = User({"name": "John"}, storage)

storage.make_relation(
    from_=john,
    to_=address,
    relation_type=RelationType.PARENT,
)

assert john.address == address

storage.remove_relation(
    from_=john,
    to_=address,
    relation_type=RelationType.PARENT,
)

assert john.address is None
